lessons.title: War & the Soldier's Experience
lessons.description: How Owen, Tennyson and Hardy present the soldier's experience of battle, duty, futility and horror.
lessons.content_html:
War Through the Soldier’s Eyes

Three poems in the Edexcel Conflict anthology examine what it feels like to be a soldier in battle. Exposure by Wilfred Owen, The Charge of the Light Brigade by Alfred Lord Tennyson, and The Man He Killed by Thomas Hardy each offer radically different perspectives on war — from the grinding misery of the trenches, to the glory and horror of a cavalry charge, to the quiet absurdity of killing a stranger. Together they show us how poets use language and structure to shape our response to conflict.

Key Fact

Owen’s Exposure was written from the trenches of World War I. Its central message is that the soldiers’ worst enemy is not the opposing army but the relentless, deadly cold. The refrain “But nothing happens” emphasises futility — these men suffer and die without even engaging in battle.

Exposure — Wilfred Owen (1917–18)

Owen served in the trenches and was killed one week before the Armistice. Exposure describes soldiers waiting in freezing conditions through the night. Nature — wind, snow, frost — is personified as an active attacker: “merciless iced east winds that knive us.” The verb ‘knive’ turns weather into a weapon, suggesting nature is more dangerous than any enemy soldier.

The soldiers hallucinate about home — “Slowly our ghosts drag home” — suggesting they are already psychologically dead. Owen uses rhetorical questions (“What are we doing here?”) to voice their despair. The half-rhymes throughout (“knive us … nervous,” “wire … war”) create a dissonant, unsettling sound that mirrors the soldiers’ unease.

The final stanza is devastating. Owen writes “For love of God seems dying” — faith itself is a casualty of the war. The closing image of the dead being buried with “half-known faces” dehumanises them; they are so frozen and disfigured they are barely recognisable. The repeated refrain “But nothing happens” closes the poem with crushing futility — all this suffering achieves nothing.

The Charge of the Light Brigade — Alfred Lord Tennyson (1854)

Tennyson wrote this poem in response to a newspaper report about a disastrous cavalry charge during the Crimean War. Due to a miscommunicated order, 600 British cavalrymen charged directly into Russian artillery. Tennyson both celebrates their bravery and criticises the officers’ blunder: “Someone had blundered.”

The driving dactylic rhythm (“HALF a league, HALF a league, HALF a league ONward”) mimics the thundering hooves of the horses. Repetition of “valley of Death” and “cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them” surrounds the reader with danger, just as the soldiers were surrounded. Tennyson honours obedience (“Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die”) while simultaneously exposing the futility of following orders that lead to slaughter.

The Man He Killed — Thomas Hardy (1902)

Hardy wrote this dramatic monologue from the perspective of an ordinary soldier reflecting on killing an enemy during the Boer War. The speaker realises that in any other situation, the man he killed could have been his friend: “Had he and I but met / By some old ancient inn, / We should have sat us down to wet / Right many a nipperkin!”

The conversational tone and simple ballad form (ABAB rhyme, regular metre) contrast sharply with the gravity of the subject. The dashes and hesitations in “I shot him dead because — / Because he was my foe” reveal the speaker struggling to justify his actions. The repetition of “because” sounds unconvincing, as though the speaker himself does not believe his own reasoning.

Key Fact

Hardy’s speaker reveals that both he and the enemy enlisted because they were out of work: “He thought he’d ’list, perhaps, / Off-hand like — just as I.” This highlights how war exploits the poor — men with no personal quarrel kill each other because they have no other options.

Perspective on duty: Tennyson glorifies obedience (“Theirs not to reason why”), while Owen and Hardy both question it. Owen’s soldiers endure pointless suffering; Hardy’s speaker realises the absurdity of killing a stranger for a cause he doesn’t understand.

Tone: Tennyson uses an elevated, heroic register; Owen is bleak, cold and despairing; Hardy is conversational and darkly ironic. These tonal differences shape how the reader responds emotionally to each poem.

Form: Tennyson’s galloping dactyls drive forward with energy. Owen’s half-rhymes and long stanzas create a dragging, exhausting feel. Hardy’s neat ballad stanzas feel deceptively simple, which makes the moral complexity more shocking.

Exam Focus: AO2 + AO3

In the Edexcel exam (Component 2, Section B Part 1), you will be given a named poem printed in the booklet and asked to compare it with one poem of your choice from the anthology. You must discuss how language and structure create meaning (AO2) and the influence of context on the poems (AO3). For these three poems, strong AO3 points include: Owen’s first-hand trench experience, Tennyson’s response to a real news report within weeks of the event, and Hardy’s pacifist beliefs shaped by the Boer War.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the Edexcel comparison, the named poem is printed — but you must recall quotations from your chosen poem from memory. Pick a poem you know well enough to quote from confidently. When comparing, always explain how the poets achieve their effects (AO2) and why their historical context matters (AO3). A strong paragraph might say: “Owen uses personification of nature to convey the futility of trench warfare, whereas Tennyson uses a driving dactylic rhythm to honour the soldiers’ bravery during the Crimean War.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exposure uses personification, half-rhyme and the refrain “But nothing happens” to convey the futility and deadly boredom of trench warfare.
  • The Charge of the Light Brigade uses dactylic rhythm, repetition and a heroic register to celebrate courage while exposing the incompetence of commanders.
  • The Man He Killed uses a simple ballad form and hesitant dashes to reveal the absurdity of killing a man who could have been a friend.

lessons.title: The Impact of War on Others
lessons.description: How Weir, Satyamurti and Levertov present the impact of war on civilians — grief, remembrance and erasure.
lessons.content_html:
War Beyond the Battlefield

Not all conflict poetry is written from the soldier’s perspective. Three poems in the Edexcel Conflict anthology focus on the people left behind or affected indirectly: Poppies by Jane Weir explores a mother’s grief as her son leaves for war; War Photographer by Carole Satyamurti examines how witnessing conflict through a lens creates moral and emotional conflict; and What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov asks what happens to an entire culture when it is destroyed by war.

Key Fact

Jane Weir’s Poppies was commissioned by the Poetry Archive in 2009 as part of a collection responding to conflict. It draws on the experience of mothers whose children serve in the armed forces, and blends domestic imagery with the symbolism of Remembrance Day.

Poppies — Jane Weir

The poem is narrated by a mother who pins a poppy on her son’s lapel before he leaves — possibly for war, possibly for the last time. The domestic details are heartbreaking: she resists the urge to “run my fingers through the gelled / blackthorns of your hair” and later smooths down his “shirt’s upturned collar.” These small, physical gestures convey a love she cannot express in words.

Weir uses a extended metaphor of textiles throughout: “I pinned one onto your lapel, crimped petals,” “sellotape bandaged around my hand,” “the world overflowing like a treasure chest.” The textile imagery connects the mother’s domestic world (sewing, fabric) to the military world (the poppy, the bandage). The word “crimped” suggests something carefully made by hand — fragile, easily damaged.

The poem ends with the mother at a war memorial, pressing her ear against it “hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind.” The enjambment here mirrors her reaching out emotionally across the distance. “Playground voice” reminds us he is still her child, regardless of his age, and the verb “catching” suggests the voice is fragile and fleeting, barely there.

Weir deliberately blurs the timeline. The poem shifts between memories of the son as a child (“playground voice,” “All Hallows’ Day”) and the present moment of him leaving. This non-linear structure reflects how grief works — the mother’s mind moves between past and present, unable to separate the child she raised from the soldier he has become. The lack of a clear narrative resolution mirrors the unresolved nature of her grief.

War Photographer — Carole Satyamurti

Satyamurti’s War Photographer (not to be confused with Carol Ann Duffy’s poem of the same title) presents a photographer who documents conflict zones. The poem explores the moral dilemma of witnessing suffering: should the photographer help, or does their role demand they remain detached and document the truth?

The photographer captures an image of a dying man: “The reassurance of the frame” — a distancing mechanism that allows the photographer to cope. The “frame” creates a protected window on suffering. Yet the “reassurance” is fragile: the photographs force them to confront what they witnessed later, in the safety of the darkroom.

Satyamurti uses the metaphor of the camera as a “reflecting eye” — it mirrors reality but also distances the viewer from it. The poem questions whether photography can truly convey suffering, or whether it reduces human agony to a flat, consumable image. This links to AO3: the role of media in shaping public understanding of conflict.

What Were They Like? — Denise Levertov (1966)

Levertov wrote this poem in protest against the Vietnam War. It is structured as a Q&A: six numbered questions about Vietnamese culture are followed by six numbered answers. The questions ask about Vietnamese customs, art, ceremonies and language. The answers reveal that all of it has been destroyed.

The Q&A format is clinically detached — it reads like an anthropological survey about an extinct civilisation. This is deliberate: Levertov forces the reader to confront the idea that an entire living culture has been reduced to a historical curiosity. The past tense throughout (“Did they use bone and ivory?”) treats the Vietnamese as already gone, which is both accusatory and deeply unsettling.

Key Fact

Levertov’s answers grow increasingly emotional: “Sir, laughter is bitter to the burned mouth.” The word “Sir” is formally polite but also accusatory — it addresses the powerful people who ordered the destruction. The metaphor “bitter to the burned mouth” is visceral, connecting the physical horror of napalm to the death of joy itself.

Grief (Poppies): Weir focuses on individual, private loss — one mother’s unspoken love for her child. The conflict is internal: the struggle between letting go and holding on.

Moral conflict (War Photographer): Satyamurti explores the ethical tension between documenting suffering and being complicit in it. The photographer’s conflict is professional and personal.

Cultural erasure (What Were They Like?): Levertov addresses the largest scale — the destruction of an entire people’s identity. The conflict is political and collective.

All three poems show that war’s damage extends far beyond the battlefield. In the exam, comparing the scale of impact (individual vs collective) is a strong analytical move.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Edexcel exam, you will have the named poem in front of you but must recall your chosen poem from memory. If Poppies, War Photographer or What Were They Like? is printed, choose one of the others as your comparison — you already know they share the theme of civilian perspectives on conflict. Focus your comparison on scale (personal vs political), tone (tender vs accusatory vs detached), and form (free verse vs Q&A structure). Always ground your analysis in AO2 (how language/structure creates meaning) and AO3 (the poets’ contexts and intentions).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Poppies uses textile imagery, enjambment and a non-linear timeline to convey a mother’s unspoken grief and the blurred boundary between past and present.
  • War Photographer explores the moral dilemma of witnessing suffering through a camera lens — the viewfinder both protects and implicates the photographer.
  • What Were They Like? uses a clinical Q&A structure to protest the cultural destruction of Vietnam, treating a living civilisation as though it were already extinct.

lessons.title: Inner Conflict & Anger
lessons.description: How Blake, Wordsworth and Rossetti present inner conflict — suppressed anger, nature's power and betrayal.
lessons.content_html:
Conflict Within

Not all conflict involves armies and battlefields. Three poems in the Edexcel Conflict anthology explore internal struggles: A Poison Tree by William Blake examines how suppressed anger grows into something destructive; Extract from The Prelude ‘Boating’ by William Wordsworth dramatises a terrifying encounter with the power of nature; and Cousin Kate by Christina Rossetti voices a woman’s fury at being used and discarded by a powerful man. Each poem shows how inner conflict can be just as devastating as physical violence.

A Poison Tree — William Blake (1794)

Blake was a Romantic poet who challenged the rigid social and religious structures of his time. A Poison Tree is an allegory about the dangers of suppressed anger. The speaker tells his friend about his wrath and it ends; he hides his anger from his enemy and it grows.

Blake uses the extended metaphor of a tree to chart the growth of hidden rage. The speaker “waterd it in fears, / Night & morning with my tears” and “sunned it with smiles, / And with soft deceitful wiles.” The natural imagery of watering and sunlight is ironic — nurturing language is applied to something toxic. The anger grows until it bears “an apple bright” which the speaker’s enemy steals and eats, and is found “outstretchd beneath the tree” — dead.

Key Fact

The “apple bright” is a biblical allusion to the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden. Just as the serpent tempted Eve, the speaker’s suppressed anger creates a deadly temptation. Blake implies that dishonesty and repression are more destructive than honest confrontation.

The poem has four quatrains with a simple AABB rhyme scheme and regular rhythm, giving it the feel of a nursery rhyme or children’s fable. This simplicity is deceptive — the childlike form makes the dark subject matter (murder through deceit) even more disturbing. The contrast between innocent form and sinister content is itself a kind of conflict. Each stanza advances the narrative one step: anger expressed, anger concealed, anger growing, enemy destroyed.

Extract from The Prelude ‘Boating’ — William Wordsworth

Wordsworth’s autobiographical epic The Prelude (published 1850) traces the development of his mind and imagination. This extract describes a boy stealing a boat at night and rowing across a lake. At first, the experience is joyful: “lustily / I dipped my oars into the silent lake.” But as he rows further, a “huge peak, black and huge” seems to rise from behind the smaller hills and pursue him.

The conflict here is between the boy’s confidence and nature’s overwhelming power. Wordsworth personifies the mountain: it “Strode after me” with “measured motion like a living thing.” The boy is terrified and rows back “with trembling oars.” For days after, his mind is haunted by “huge and mighty forms, that do not live / Like living men.” Nature has permanently altered his understanding of himself.

Key Fact

Wordsworth wrote this as blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter. The lack of rhyme and stanza breaks creates a continuous, unbroken flow that mirrors the boy’s rowing and the relentless advance of the mountain. The form reinforces the sense of an experience that overwhelms normal structures of thought.

Cousin Kate — Christina Rossetti (1862)

Rossetti writes from the perspective of a “cottage maiden” who was seduced and abandoned by a lord. The lord then married her cousin Kate instead. The speaker is left shamed and outcast: “The neighbours call me an unclean thing.” Her anger is directed at both the lord (“He lured me to his palace home”) and at Kate (“O cousin Kate, my love was true”).

The ballad form (ABCB rhyme, regular metre) gives the poem a folk-song quality, which suits its story of love, betrayal and social injustice. Rossetti uses possessive language to show how the lord treats women as property: “He wore me like a silken knot, / He changed me like a glove.” The similes reduce the speaker to an object — decorative, disposable, easily replaced.

The poem’s final twist is powerful: the speaker has a son (“my fair-haired son, my shame, my pride”), while Kate remains childless. In Victorian society, producing an heir was a woman’s most important role. The speaker’s “shame” (an illegitimate child) becomes her triumph — she has something Kate, for all her status, lacks.

Blake (A Poison Tree): The conflict is between expressing and suppressing emotion. Blake argues that repression breeds something far worse than honest anger — it breeds calculated cruelty.

Wordsworth (The Prelude): The conflict is between human confidence and nature’s sublime, terrifying power. The boy’s self-assurance is destroyed by an encounter he cannot control or understand.

Rossetti (Cousin Kate): The conflict is between a woman’s love and the patriarchal society that exploits and discards her. The speaker channels her betrayal into defiant pride.

All three poets are from the Romantic or Victorian period. A strong AO3 response would discuss how each reflects the tensions of their era: Blake’s challenge to religious repression, Wordsworth’s worship of the sublime, and Rossetti’s critique of Victorian gender inequality.
lessons.exam_tip_html: These three poems work well as comparison pairs because they share the theme of inner conflict but differ hugely in tone, form and focus. In the exam, if one of these is the named poem, consider choosing another from this group. For example: compare Blake’s allegorical treatment of suppressed anger with Rossetti’s dramatic monologue of personal betrayal. Both present destructive emotions, but Blake’s is coldly calculated while Rossetti’s is raw and passionate. Always link your analysis to AO2 (specific language and structural choices) and AO3 (what the poets’ contexts reveal about their intentions).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A Poison Tree uses an extended tree metaphor and deceptively simple rhyme to show how suppressed anger grows into deadly violence.
  • Extract from The Prelude uses blank verse, personification and the shift from joy to terror to dramatise the overwhelming power of nature.
  • Cousin Kate uses ballad form, possessive similes and a defiant final twist to voice a woman’s anger at sexual exploitation and social hypocrisy.

lessons.title: Social Conflict & Identity
lessons.description: How Agard, Zephaniah, Casey and Carson use language to challenge racism, class prejudice and sectarianism.
lessons.content_html:
Language as a Weapon and a Shield

Four poems in the Edexcel Conflict anthology explore social conflict — the everyday battles over identity, race, class and belonging. Half-caste by John Agard challenges racial categorisation; No Problem by Benjamin Zephaniah confronts racism with defiant humour; The Class Game by Mary Casey attacks class snobbery; and Belfast Confetti by Ciaran Carson fragments language itself to convey the chaos of sectarian violence. In each poem, language is both the subject and the weapon.

Half-caste — John Agard

Agard, born in Guyana and living in Britain, wrote Half-caste to challenge the term “half-caste,” which was used to describe people of mixed heritage. The poem is a sustained rhetorical attack on the absurdity of the label. Agard asks: if Picasso mixes red and green, is that a “half-caste canvas”? If Tchaikovsky blends a black key and a white key, is that a “half-caste symphony”?

These examples expose the ridiculousness of calling a person “half” anything. The colloquial Caribbean dialect (“Explain yuself / wha yu mean”) is a deliberate political choice: Agard refuses to adopt “standard English” because doing so would accept the hierarchy that labels him as inferior. His dialect is his identity, and using it is an act of resistance.

Key Fact

Agard writes without punctuation or standard capitalisation throughout. This rejection of conventional English grammar mirrors his rejection of the social conventions that label him “half.” The form of the poem enacts the argument: if you refuse to accept someone as whole, why should they accept your rules?

Agard takes the logic of “half-caste” to absurd extremes: if he is only half a person, does he “cast half a shadow” and “dream half a dream”? This satire forces the listener to confront how dehumanising the term is. The poem ends with a challenge: “but yu must come back tomorrow / wid de whole of yu eye / an de whole of yu ear / an de whole of yu mind.” Agard demands that the listener engage with him fully — as a complete person, not a category.

No Problem — Benjamin Zephaniah

Zephaniah, a British-Jamaican dub poet, wrote No Problem as a direct response to everyday racism in Britain. The speaker lists the prejudices he faces — “I am not de problem” — and turns each accusation back on the accuser. The repetition of “I am not de problem” is both a denial and an assertion of identity.

The poem’s rhythm is rooted in dub culture — a blend of reggae and spoken word. Read aloud, the poem has a musical, almost chant-like quality that turns protest into performance. Zephaniah uses humour (“I am born academic”) and defiance (“Black is not de problem”) together, refusing to be defined by others’ prejudice. The final message is clear: racism is the problem of the racist, not the victim.

The Class Game — Mary Casey

Casey’s poem attacks class snobbery in Britain by listing the markers used to judge someone’s social status: “How can you tell what class I’m from? / I can tell by your hands.” She catalogues the differences between working-class and middle-class life: “a deck chair, or a yacht,” “a corgi, or a whippet.” The poem’s listing technique builds an overwhelming case that class divisions are arbitrary and absurd.

Casey writes in a strong working-class voice, using dialect and colloquial language (“me mam,” “bog standard”). Like Agard, her refusal to adopt “proper” English is politically charged — she speaks as she is, rejecting the idea that her accent or vocabulary makes her inferior. The poem’s direct address (“How can you tell?”) confronts the reader, demanding they examine their own prejudices.

Belfast Confetti — Ciaran Carson

Carson writes about the Troubles in Northern Ireland. “Belfast confetti” was a slang term for the shrapnel — nuts, bolts, nails — packed into homemade bombs. The poem describes a bomb explosion and its aftermath, but what makes it extraordinary is how Carson uses punctuation marks as shrapnel.

“Suddenly as the riot squad moved in it was raining exclamation marks, / Nuts, bolts, nails, car keys. A fount of broken type.” The metaphor of punctuation as debris is brilliant: the explosion shatters language itself. The speaker cannot complete a sentence: “I know this labyrinth so well — / Balaklava, Raglan, Inkerman, Odessa Street —” The dashes interrupt thought, just as the violence interrupts life. Even the street names reference the Crimean War, layering historical conflict onto present-day Belfast.

Key Fact

Carson ends with a flurry of unanswered questions: “What is / My name? Where am I coming from? Where am I going?” The violence has stripped the speaker of his most basic certainties — identity, origin, direction. The poem’s fragmented form mirrors the fragmentation of the speaker’s mind and city.

Agard and Zephaniah both use Caribbean dialect as an act of resistance against Standard English. Their poems are performed as much as read — the oral tradition is part of their identity and politics.

Casey uses working-class dialect for the same purpose: refusing to speak “properly” is itself a challenge to the class system.

Carson shows language breaking down under violence — rather than using language as a weapon of resistance, he shows how conflict destroys the ability to communicate at all.

In the exam, these poems pair well together for comparisons about how language and form reflect identity and resistance. Agard + Casey is a particularly strong pairing: both reject “standard” language conventions to challenge prejudice (racial vs class).
lessons.exam_tip_html: These poems reward close analysis of form (AO2). Agard’s lack of punctuation, Zephaniah’s dub rhythm, Casey’s working-class voice and Carson’s fragmented sentences all demonstrate how the way a poem is written can be as important as what it says. In the exam, always link form to meaning: “Agard rejects standard punctuation to mirror his rejection of the social conventions that label him as ‘half.’” For AO3, discuss how each poet’s personal or cultural context shapes their use of language: Agard’s Guyanese heritage, Zephaniah’s Jamaican-British identity, Casey’s working-class background, Carson’s experience of the Troubles.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Half-caste uses Caribbean dialect, satire and the rejection of punctuation to challenge racial categorisation and demand full recognition as a human being.
  • No Problem uses dub rhythm, repetition and humour to confront racism and assert that prejudice is the racist’s problem, not the victim’s.
  • The Class Game uses listing, direct address and working-class dialect to expose the arbitrary markers of class division.
  • Belfast Confetti uses fragmented punctuation as a metaphor for shrapnel, showing how sectarian violence destroys language, identity and the ability to think clearly.

lessons.title: Destruction & Violence
lessons.description: How Byron, Carson and Clarke present destruction — divine wrath, urban violence and the conflict of motherhood.
lessons.content_html:
Destruction in Three Forms

Destruction takes many shapes in the Edexcel Conflict anthology. The Destruction of Sennacherib by Lord Byron presents divine violence as unstoppable and absolute. Belfast Confetti by Ciaran Carson captures the moment of a bomb explosion in a city torn apart by sectarian conflict. Catrin by Gillian Clarke explores a different kind of conflict entirely — the physical and emotional struggle of giving birth, and the ongoing battle of wills between mother and daughter. All three poems use form and language to convey how destruction fragments the world.

The Destruction of Sennacherib — Lord Byron (1815)

Byron retells the biblical story (2 Kings 19) of the Assyrian king Sennacherib, whose army besieged Jerusalem and was destroyed overnight by the Angel of the Lord. Byron presents the Assyrian army in its full glory before showing its sudden, total annihilation — a reminder that no military power can withstand divine judgement.

The poem’s driving anapaestic rhythm (“The As-SYR-ian came DOWN like the WOLF on the FOLD”) creates a galloping energy that mirrors the cavalry charge. The simile “like the wolf on the fold” presents the Assyrians as predators — powerful, aggressive and dangerous. Yet within six stanzas, that power is completely destroyed.

Key Fact

Byron uses vivid colour imagery to chart the destruction. The army arrives in “purple and gold” — colours of royalty and wealth. The next morning, the soldiers are pale and lifeless: “the eyes of the sleepers waxed deadly and chill, / And their hearts but once heaved, and for ever grew still.” The contrast between vibrant life and sudden death makes the destruction feel swift and absolute.

Byron structures the poem as a narrative of decline. Stanza 1: the army charges, glittering and powerful. Stanza 2: the Angel of Death arrives “and breathed in the face of the foe as he passed.” Stanza 3: the next morning, the army is dead. The subsequent stanzas dwell on the aftermath — the horse with “distended” nostrils, the abandoned weapons, the widows of Ashur. Each couplet advances the destruction, so the relentless rhyme scheme (AABB) feels like a drumbeat of doom.

Belfast Confetti — Ciaran Carson (Revisited)

Carson’s poem (covered in detail in Lesson 4) is also a study in physical destruction — but of a city, not an army. Where Byron’s destruction is swift, divine and absolute, Carson’s is human, chaotic and ongoing. The “fount of broken type” scatters across the poem like debris across a street. Street names from the Crimean War (“Balaklava, Raglan, Inkerman”) layer historical conflict onto present-day Belfast, suggesting that destruction repeats through history.

Formally, Carson’s fragmented free verse is the opposite of Byron’s driving couplets. Byron’s regular form conveys an ordered, purposeful destruction from God; Carson’s chaotic form conveys the disorder and randomness of a bomb blast. Comparing these two approaches to destruction is an excellent exam strategy.

Catrin — Gillian Clarke

Clarke’s Catrin describes the moment of her daughter’s birth and the ongoing conflict of the mother-daughter relationship. The poem opens in a hospital room: “I can remember you, child, / As I stood in a hot, white / Room at the window watching.” The birth is presented not as a tender moment but as a battle: “I wrote / All over the walls with my / Words, coloured the clean squares / With the wild, tender circles / Of our first fierce confrontation.”

The symbol of the “tight / Red rope of love” — the umbilical cord — runs through the poem. It represents the physical and emotional bond between mother and child. Clarke calls it a “rope” rather than a cord, suggesting something stronger and more combative — like a tug-of-war. Even after the cord is cut, the conflict continues: “Still I am fighting / You off.”

Key Fact

The poem is divided into two stanzas: the first describes the birth; the second jumps to the present, where the daughter wants to “skate / In the dark, for one more hour.” This structural division mirrors the two stages of the conflict — the physical struggle of birth and the emotional struggle of letting go as the child grows independent.

Scale: Byron presents the annihilation of an entire army — destruction on a biblical scale. Carson focuses on one moment in one street — a single explosion that shatters a local world. Clarke’s “destruction” is the most intimate: the severing of the umbilical cord, which is both a physical separation and the beginning of a lifelong emotional battle.

Form: Byron’s driving AABB couplets and anapaestic rhythm convey ordered, purposeful devastation. Carson’s fragmented free verse conveys chaos and confusion. Clarke’s two-stanza structure mirrors the two stages of the mother-child conflict (birth and growing up).

Agent of destruction: Byron: God. Carson: human sectarianism. Clarke: the natural, inevitable process of a child separating from a parent. Each poet shows that destruction is not always negative — Clarke’s “conflict” is born from love.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Catrin is often underestimated as a “conflict” poem because it deals with parenthood rather than war. In the exam, choosing Catrin as your comparison poem can earn high marks precisely because it demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of what conflict means. If the named poem is about war, you can argue: “Clarke shows that conflict is not limited to the battlefield — the ‘fierce confrontation’ of birth and the ongoing tug-of-war between mother and daughter are just as intense, though the ‘red rope of love’ transforms destruction into connection.” This kind of unexpected comparison impresses examiners.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Destruction of Sennacherib uses anapaestic rhythm, colour imagery and AABB couplets to convey the swift, absolute annihilation of a mighty army by divine power.
  • Belfast Confetti uses punctuation as shrapnel and fragmented free verse to capture the chaos of a bomb explosion and the destruction of language, thought and identity.
  • Catrin uses the extended symbol of the “red rope of love” and a two-stanza structure to present birth and motherhood as a form of conflict — fierce but rooted in love.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Byron uses the simile 'like the wolf on the fold' in the opening of The Destruction of Sennacherib.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- 'Wolf' presents the Assyrian army as predatory, aggressive and dangerous (1 mark)
- 'Fold' refers to a flock of sheep — the Israelites are presented as vulnerable and defenceless (1 mark)
- The simile establishes the power imbalance: a mighty predator vs helpless prey, which makes the subsequent divine destruction even more dramatic (1 mark)
- Links to the biblical context: God defends the weak against the powerful, overturning the expected outcome (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Clarke present the conflict of motherhood in Catrin? You should consider language, form and structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The 'tight / Red rope of love' (umbilical cord) is both a bond and a battleground — 'rope' suggests tug-of-war rather than tenderness. The two-stanza structure mirrors two stages: physical separation at birth and emotional separation as the child grows. 'First fierce confrontation' uses alliteration to stress intensity. The present-tense 'Still I am fighting / You off' shows the conflict is ongoing — motherhood is a perpetual negotiation between holding on and letting go.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the mother-daughter conflict.
Lower band (1-2): Simple description.

practice_questions.text: Compare how destruction is presented in The Destruction of Sennacherib and Belfast Confetti. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained, convincing comparison. Byron's destruction is divine, ordered and absolute — AABB couplets and anapaestic rhythm drive relentlessly forward. Carson's is human, chaotic and random — fragmented free verse mirrors a bomb blast. Byron's colour imagery tracks from life (purple/gold) to death (pale/still); Carson's punctuation metaphor shows language itself shattering. Byron retells a biblical story to celebrate divine power; Carson writes from personal experience of the Troubles to convey its psychological impact.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis of methods.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, limited analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: How does Byron use the anapaestic metre in The Destruction of Sennacherib to convey the experience of the cavalry charge?
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- The anapaestic rhythm (da-da-DUM, da-da-DUM) creates a galloping, energetic beat that mimics horses charging (1 mark)
- The regularity of the metre gives the poem a relentless, unstoppable momentum — like the army itself (1 mark)
- This energy makes the sudden destruction more dramatic: the same rhythm that conveyed power now conveys collapse (1 mark)
- Links to the poem's narrative arc: the driving rhythm carries the reader from the army's arrival through to its annihilation without pause (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Clarke uses the symbol of the 'red rope of love' throughout Catrin. How does this single image capture the poem's central conflict?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The 'rope' is the umbilical cord — literally connecting mother and child. 'Red' connotes blood, passion and danger, suggesting the bond is intense and visceral. 'Love' softens the imagery, but 'rope' also suggests restraint, tug-of-war and bondage. The oxymoronic quality captures the poem's core truth: the mother-child relationship is simultaneously loving and combative. The rope is physically cut at birth but emotionally persists — 'Still I am fighting / You off' — showing separation is never complete.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of the symbol.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding of the metaphor.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: How does Byron use colour imagery in The Destruction of Sennacherib to chart the shift from power to death? Refer to specific quotations.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. 'Purple and gold' in the opening connote royalty, wealth and military splendour. The army's 'cohorts gleaming' suggests they are dazzling and magnificent. By the morning, the soldiers' eyes are 'deadly and chill' — warmth has been replaced by cold. The 'widows of Ashur are loud in their wail' shifts focus from the army's glory to human grief. The colour journey (vibrant → pale → absent) parallels the journey from life to death, from power to oblivion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of colour shift.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some identification of colour imagery.
Lower band (1-2): Basic observations.

lessons.title: Form, Structure & Language
lessons.description: Master the key poetic forms, structures and language techniques used across all 15 Conflict poems.
lessons.content_html:
Why Form and Structure Matter

In the Edexcel exam, AO2 requires you to analyse how poets use language, form and structure to create meaning. This lesson gives you a toolkit of key techniques across all 15 Conflict poems, so you can identify and analyse them confidently under exam conditions. Understanding why a poet chose a particular form is just as important as spotting it.

Poetic Forms in the Anthology

Key Fact

The Conflict anthology contains five main poetic forms: ballad (The Man He Killed, Cousin Kate, The Charge of the Light Brigade), dramatic monologue (The Man He Killed, Cousin Kate, Half-caste), free verse (Belfast Confetti, Poppies, War Photographer), blank verse (The Prelude), and song/chant (No Problem, The Class Game). Each form shapes how the reader experiences the conflict.

A ballad tells a story with a regular rhythm and rhyme. In the anthology, Hardy’s The Man He Killed uses ABAB ballad metre to tell a simple story with devastating moral complexity — the neat form makes the messy reality of killing even more unsettling. Rossetti’s Cousin Kate uses the ballad’s folk-song tradition to voice a wronged woman’s story, connecting her personal betrayal to a long tradition of songs about love and injustice. Tennyson’s The Charge of the Light Brigade uses a modified ballad form with a driving dactylic rhythm to create the energy of a cavalry charge.

A dramatic monologue gives us one voice speaking directly. Hardy’s soldier in The Man He Killed reveals his guilt and confusion through hesitation. Rossetti’s speaker in Cousin Kate reveals her anger and defiance. Agard’s speaker in Half-caste directly confronts the reader with questions they cannot comfortably answer. In each case, the single voice creates intimacy and forces the reader to engage with a perspective they might otherwise dismiss.

Free verse (no regular metre or rhyme) is used by Carson (Belfast Confetti), Weir (Poppies) and Satyamurti (War Photographer). Free verse allows the poet to vary rhythm for effect — Carson’s fragmented lines mirror a bomb blast; Weir’s flowing enjambment mirrors a mother’s uncontrolled grief. Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) is used by Wordsworth in The Prelude extract, creating a continuous, elevated tone suited to the sublime encounter with nature.

Key Structural Techniques

Enjambment is used by Weir in Poppies (“hoping to hear / your playground voice”) to create a reaching, breathless quality. Owen uses it in Exposure to drag lines out, mirroring the endless waiting. In contrast, caesura creates abrupt pauses: Carson’s dashes in Belfast Confetti halt thought mid-sentence; Owen’s “But nothing happens.” ends each stanza with crushing finality.

Refrain is used powerfully by Owen (“But nothing happens” in Exposure) and Zephaniah (“I am not de problem” in No Problem). In Owen, the refrain reinforces futility — nothing changes despite the suffering. In Zephaniah, it builds an assertive, defiant rhythm that turns denial into empowerment.

Key Fact

The same technique can create completely different effects depending on the poem. Enjambment in Poppies creates emotional overflow (a mother’s uncontrolled grief); enjambment in Exposure creates a dragging, exhausting feel (endless trench waiting). Always explain the specific effect in the poem you are analysing, not just name the technique.

Key Language Techniques Across the Anthology

Personification: Owen personifies nature as an attacker in Exposure (“merciless iced east winds that knive us”). Wordsworth personifies the mountain in The Prelude (“Strode after me”). Both use personification to show nature’s power over humanity, but Owen’s is hostile while Wordsworth’s is awe-inspiring.

Metaphor and simile: Byron’s “like the wolf on the fold” establishes the Assyrians as predators. Clarke’s “red rope of love” captures the oxymoronic nature of motherhood. Blake’s poison tree is a sustained allegory for suppressed anger. Carson’s punctuation-as-shrapnel metaphor is one of the most original in the anthology.

Dialect and register: Agard, Zephaniah and Casey all use non-standard English as an act of resistance. Hardy’s speaker uses colloquial, working-class language (“’list,” “nipperkin”) to show the soldier is an ordinary man, not a hero. Tennyson’s elevated, heroic register (“Noble six hundred!”) celebrates bravery. The register a poet chooses shapes the reader’s emotional response to the conflict.

Full rhyme is used by Blake (AABB in A Poison Tree), Byron (AABB in Sennacherib) and Hardy (ABAB in The Man He Killed). Regular rhyme can create a sense of inevitability (Byron) or deceptive simplicity (Blake, Hardy).

Half-rhyme (also called pararhyme) is Owen’s signature technique in Exposure: “knive us / nervous,” “wire / war.” The imperfect rhymes deny the reader a satisfying resolution, mirroring the soldiers’ denied expectations of heroism or purpose.

Repetition drives home key ideas: Tennyson’s “cannon to right … left … front” surrounds the reader with danger; Agard’s “Explain yuself” demands answers; Owen’s “But nothing happens” crushes hope with each return.

Applying This to the Exam

In the Edexcel comparison (Component 2, Section B Part 1), you must compare the named poem with one you have chosen. The strongest responses integrate form, structure and language analysis (AO2) throughout — not in a separate paragraph at the end. A useful pattern is: what (identify the technique) → how (explain its effect) → why (link to the poet’s intention or context). For example: “Owen uses half-rhyme [what] to deny the reader a satisfying resolution [how], reflecting the soldiers’ own denied expectations of heroism in the futility of trench warfare [why].”
lessons.exam_tip_html: Do not write a separate “form and structure” paragraph in the exam. Instead, weave structural analysis into every point you make. If you are discussing Owen’s presentation of futility, analyse the refrain “But nothing happens” alongside his language choices. If you are comparing Carson and Byron, discuss how their contrasting forms (fragmented vs driving) reflect contrasting types of destruction. This integrated approach shows the examiner that you understand how form and content work together — which is exactly what AO2 rewards.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The anthology uses five main forms: ballad, dramatic monologue, free verse, blank verse and song/chant. Each form shapes how the reader experiences the conflict.
  • Enjambment, caesura, refrain and rhyme scheme are the most important structural techniques. The same technique can create very different effects depending on the poem.
  • In the exam, integrate form and structure analysis into every paragraph — use the what → how → why pattern to ensure your analysis is precise and purposeful.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Owen uses half-rhyme in Exposure and Blake uses full rhyme in A Poison Tree. How does each poet's rhyme scheme reinforce their poem's message?
practice_questions.marks:

Blake's AABB full rhymes create a nursery-rhyme simplicity that makes the dark content (murder through deceit) more disturbing — the innocent form conflicts with sinister meaning. Both poets use rhyme as a tool of meaning, not just decoration.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear comparison with some analysis of effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how enjambment is used differently in Poppies (Weir) and Exposure (Owen). Refer to specific examples.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- In Poppies, enjambment ('hoping to hear / your playground voice') creates a breathless, reaching quality — the mother's emotion overflows the line, reflecting her uncontrolled grief (1 mark)
- In Exposure, enjambment drags lines out, creating a heavy, exhausting rhythm that mirrors the soldiers' endless waiting in the trenches (1 mark)
- Both use enjambment to reflect emotional states, but Weir's is active (reaching out) while Owen's is passive (enduring) (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does the use of non-standard English in Half-caste, No Problem and The Class Game function as an act of resistance? Compare at least two poems. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. All three poets refuse to adopt 'standard' English, which is itself a political statement: accepting the rules of a culture that marginalises you means accepting your marginalisation. Agard's Caribbean dialect and lack of punctuation reject the conventions of the culture that labelled him 'half-caste.' Casey's working-class voice rejects the idea that 'proper' speech equals intelligence. Zephaniah's dub rhythm connects his poetry to Jamaican oral tradition. each poet's cultural background shapes their linguistic choices.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, basic observations.
Lower band (1-5): Limited engagement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how caesura is used in Belfast Confetti and Exposure. What different effects does it create in each poem?

- In Exposure, 'But nothing happens.' ends stanzas with a crushing, final pause that emphasises futility and hopelessness (1 mark)
- Carson's caesura creates confusion and disorder; Owen's creates resignation and defeat (1 mark)
- Both show how punctuation can be used structurally to convey psychological states — chaos in Carson, despair in Owen (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Why is Wordsworth's choice of blank verse significant for the extract from The Prelude? How does the form relate to the poem's content?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) creates a continuous, elevated tone appropriate for a profound spiritual experience. The absence of rhyme prevents predictable resolution, mirroring the boy's inability to process what he has witnessed. The lack of stanza breaks creates an unbroken flow that mirrors the boy's continuous rowing and the mountain's relentless advance. The regular metre occasionally falters when the mountain appears, reflecting the disruption to the boy's composure.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis of blank verse with some effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Basic identification of blank verse.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Tennyson's use of repetition in The Charge of the Light Brigade create the feeling of being surrounded by danger? Refer to specific examples.

- The triple repetition mirrors the three directions of enemy fire, making the danger feel overwhelming (1 mark)
- The driving rhythm means these repeated phrases feel relentless, like the bombardment itself (1 mark)

lessons.title: Comparison Skills
lessons.description: How to structure a comparison essay for Edexcel Component 2 Section B Part 1 — AO2 and AO3 integration.
lessons.content_html:
The Comparison Task

In the Edexcel English Literature exam (Component 2, Section B Part 1), you will be given one named poem from the Conflict anthology, printed in the exam booklet. You must compare it with one other poem of your choice from the same anthology. The question will focus on a theme (e.g. “the effects of conflict” or “attitudes towards war”) and you must discuss how both poets present that theme. The question is worth 20 marks, split across AO2 (language, form and structure — 15 marks) and AO3 (context — 5 marks).

Key Fact

The marks are weighted: AO2 = 15 marks (analyse the effects of language, form and structure using relevant subject terminology) and AO3 = 5 marks (show understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written). This means your analysis of how the poets write must be the main focus, with context woven in — not the other way around.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem

The named poem is printed — you can refer to it directly. Your chosen poem must be recalled from memory. This means you should:

  • Know 4–5 poems extremely well — not just themes but specific quotations, techniques and contextual details. Trying to learn all 15 is unrealistic under exam pressure.
  • Choose flexible poems that can be compared to many different themes. Exposure (Owen) works for: futility of war, nature’s power, the soldier’s experience, suffering. Half-caste (Agard) works for: identity, resistance, language as weapon, social conflict.
  • Choose poems with rich AO2 content — poems where form and language are distinctive and analysable. Belfast Confetti (punctuation metaphor), A Poison Tree (extended allegory), Cousin Kate (ballad form + possessive similes) are all excellent choices.

War & the soldier: Exposure + Charge of the Light Brigade + The Man He Killed

Impact on civilians: Poppies + What Were They Like? + War Photographer

Social conflict & identity: Half-caste + The Class Game + No Problem

Inner conflict: A Poison Tree + The Prelude + Cousin Kate + Catrin

Destruction: Sennacherib + Belfast Confetti + Exposure

You do not have to stay within these clusters. An unexpected comparison (e.g. Catrin + Exposure — both about endurance and emotional suffering) can demonstrate sophisticated thinking.

Structuring Your Response

You have approximately 35–40 minutes for this question. Spend 5 minutes planning and 30–35 minutes writing. A strong response has 4–5 comparative paragraphs, each one comparing a specific aspect of both poems.

Key Fact

Use a comparative paragraph structure: make a point about both poems in every paragraph. Do NOT write about Poem A for three paragraphs and then Poem B for three paragraphs — this is a common mistake that loses marks because there is no sustained comparison. Instead, every paragraph should contain analysis of both poems, linked by comparison connectives.

Writing a Comparative Paragraph

Here is a model structure for one paragraph:

  1. Opening statement — identify a shared theme or contrasting approach. E.g. “Both Owen and Tennyson present the reality of soldiers facing death, but while Tennyson celebrates their heroic obedience, Owen exposes the futility of their suffering.”
  2. Named poem analysis (AO2) — Quote from the named poem (it’s in front of you) and analyse the technique and its effect. E.g. “Tennyson’s dactylic rhythm in ‘Half a league, half a league, half a league onward’ mimics thundering hooves, creating a heroic momentum that propels the reader into battle alongside the soldiers.”
  3. Comparison connective — Use phrases like “In contrast,” “Similarly,” “However,” “While both poets…” to link to your chosen poem.
  4. Chosen poem analysis (AO2) — Quote from memory and analyse. E.g. “In contrast, Owen’s half-rhymes in Exposure (‘knive us / nervous’) deny the reader satisfying resolution, reflecting the soldiers’ own denied expectations of heroism.”
  5. Context (AO3) — Link to the poets’ contexts. E.g. “This difference reflects their contexts: Tennyson responded to a newspaper report as an outsider celebrating patriotism, while Owen wrote from first-hand trench experience, determined to expose what he called ‘the old Lie.’”

1. Writing about poems separately. Do not write three paragraphs on the named poem then three on your chosen poem. This is not a comparison — it’s two separate essays. Every paragraph must discuss both.

2. Feature-spotting without analysis. Identifying “Tennyson uses repetition” is not enough. You must explain the effect: “The anaphora of ‘Cannon to right / left / front’ surrounds the reader with danger, creating an immersive sense of being trapped.”

3. Context as a separate section. Do not bolt context onto the end. Weave it into your analysis: “Owen, drawing on his first-hand experience of the trenches, uses the refrain ‘But nothing happens’ to convey…”

4. Retelling the poem. The examiner knows what happens. Focus on how and why, not what.

Useful Comparison Connectives

Similarity: “Similarly,” “Likewise,” “In the same way,” “Both poets…” “Echoing this idea,” “This is also evident in…”

Difference: “In contrast,” “However,” “Conversely,” “While [Poet A]…, [Poet B]…,” “On the other hand,” “Whereas…”

Nuance: “Although both poets…, [Poet A] focuses on… while [Poet B] emphasises…,” “To some extent…, however…”
lessons.exam_tip_html: Before the exam, prepare quotation banks for your 4–5 chosen poems: 3–4 short quotations per poem, each with a technique identified and an effect explained. In the exam, when you see the named poem and the theme, quickly match your best comparison poem and plan 4–5 comparative points. Aim for 3–4 quotations from each poem in your response. The named poem’s quotations can be longer (you can see it); your chosen poem’s should be shorter and precisely memorised.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The exam is worth 20 marks: 15 for AO2 (language, form, structure) and 5 for AO3 (context). Focus on how the poets write, not what they write about.
  • Every paragraph must compare both poems — do not write about them separately.
  • Choose 4–5 flexible poems, learn short quotations from each, and practise matching them to different themes under timed conditions.

'Both Owen in Exposure and Weir in Poppies present conflict as an experience that extends far beyond the battlefield, yet while Owen focuses on the soldier enduring the physical horror of the trenches, Weir explores the emotional devastation left behind for those at home. Owen's half-rhymes and despairing refrain convey futility; Weir's enjambment and textile imagery convey uncontrolled grief.'
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear opening with comparison indicated.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Names both poems but limited comparison.
Lower band (1-2): Describes one poem only.

practice_questions.text: Compare how war is presented in The Charge of the Light Brigade and The Man He Killed. You should compare the poets' use of language, form and structure, and consider relevant contexts. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained, convincing comparison throughout. Analyses Tennyson's dactylic rhythm and heroic register vs Hardy's simple ballad form and colloquial hesitations. Explores how Tennyson both celebrates bravery ('Noble six hundred') and criticises command ('Someone had blundered') while Hardy questions the morality of killing ('because — / Because'). Tennyson as Poet Laureate responding to a newspaper report vs Hardy writing during the Boer War with pacifist sympathies. Both address duty, but from opposing perspectives — glory vs absurdity.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with analysis of methods from both poems.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, limited analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Mostly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: A student writes: 'Owen uses half-rhyme in Exposure.' Improve this by adding analysis of effect and context (AO2 + AO3).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- Identifies what the half-rhyme sounds like: e.g. 'knive us / nervous' — the sounds almost match but don't quite resolve (1 mark)
- Explains the effect: the imperfect rhymes deny the reader satisfying resolution, creating an unsettling, uneasy atmosphere (1 mark)
- Links to meaning: this mirrors the soldiers' own denied expectations — they expected heroism and purpose but found only futility (1 mark)
- Adds context: Owen wrote from first-hand trench experience, and the half-rhymes reflect the gap between the propaganda of war and its reality (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Plan a comparison essay for: 'Compare how the poets present identity and belonging in Half-caste and one other poem.' Choose your poem and write 4 comparative paragraph topic sentences.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Four clear, comparative topic sentences that establish a sustained argument. E.g. (choosing No Problem): 1. 'Both Agard and Zephaniah use non-standard English as a deliberate act of resistance against a culture that marginalises them.' 2. 'While Agard challenges the specific label half-caste through satirical examples, Zephaniah addresses broader everyday racism through repetition and defiance.' 3. 'Both poets use performance forms — Agard's direct address and Zephaniah's dub rhythm — to make their protests immediate and confrontational.' 4. 'Contextually, both write from the experience of Caribbean heritage in Britain, but Agard focuses on language as categorisation while Zephaniah focuses on language as empowerment.'
Upper-mid band (5-6): 3-4 topic sentences with clear comparison.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparative points but not fully developed.
Lower band (1-2): Limited planning.

practice_questions.text: Compare how personal loss is presented in Poppies and Cousin Kate. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider contexts. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Both poems are voiced by women experiencing loss — Weir's mother losing her son to war, Rossetti's speaker losing her status and innocence to a lord's exploitation. Weir uses free verse and enjambment to mirror uncontrolled emotion; Rossetti uses ballad form to place her story in a folk tradition of wronged women. Both use physical imagery: Weir's textile metaphor (pinning, smoothing) vs Rossetti's possessive similes ('wore me like a silken knot'). Weir's modern context (Remembrance, mothers of serving soldiers) vs Rossetti's Victorian context (sexual double standards, women as property).
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

lessons.title: Exam Technique & Key Quotations
lessons.description: Exam day strategy: timing, planning, quotation bank for all 15 Conflict poems, and a model response.
lessons.content_html:
Exam Day: Anthology Comparison

This is your final revision lesson before the exam. We will cover: the typical format of the question, a step-by-step strategy for the time you have, a quotation bank covering all 15 poems, and a model paragraph you can use as a template. Everything here is designed to be practical — techniques you can use on the day.

The Question Format

A named poem is typically printed in full. Below it, the question will ask you to compare how the poets present a particular theme in the named poem and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. You choose your comparison poem. The question assesses AO2 (language, form and structure) and AO3 (context), and a strong answer is usually several sides of A4. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark allocation and recommended length.

Key Fact

Timing strategy: spend roughly the first sixth of your time planning and the rest writing. In your plan, write down: (1) your chosen poem, (2) 3–4 comparison points, (3) key quotations from both poems, (4) one AO3 point per poem. This plan is your roadmap — it prevents you from drifting off-topic or repeating yourself.

Quotation Bank: All 15 Conflict Poems

Below is a core quotation for each poem with its key technique and theme. You do not need to memorise all 15 — focus on your 4–5 chosen poems — but having a working knowledge of the full list helps you make connections in the exam.

A Poison Tree (Blake): “I was angry with my foe: / I told it not, my wrath did grow.” Technique: Extended metaphor (tree), AABB rhyme. Theme: Suppressed anger becomes deadly. AO3: Blake challenged institutions that taught emotional repression.

The Destruction of Sennacherib (Byron): “The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold.” Technique: Simile, anapaestic rhythm. Theme: Divine destruction of military power. AO3: Biblical source (2 Kings 19); Byron’s fascination with power and its limits.

Extract from The Prelude (Wordsworth): “a huge peak, black and huge … Strode after me.” Technique: Personification, blank verse. Theme: Nature’s overwhelming power. AO3: Romantic belief in the sublime; autobiographical poem.

The Man He Killed (Hardy): “I shot him dead because — / Because he was my foe.” Technique: Caesura (dashes), ballad form. Theme: Absurdity of war; killing strangers. AO3: Hardy’s pacifism; Boer War context; working-class soldiers.

Cousin Kate (Rossetti): “He wore me like a silken knot, / He changed me like a glove.” Technique: Simile, ballad form. Theme: Sexual exploitation; defiance. AO3: Victorian sexual double standards; “fallen women.”

Exposure (Owen): “But nothing happens.” Technique: Refrain, half-rhyme, personification of nature. Theme: Futility of war; nature as the true enemy. AO3: Owen’s first-hand trench experience; died one week before the Armistice.

The Charge of the Light Brigade (Tennyson): “Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die.” Technique: Dactylic rhythm, anaphora, repetition. Theme: Heroic duty vs incompetent command. AO3: Tennyson was Poet Laureate; wrote in response to a newspaper report of the Crimean War.

Half-caste (Agard): “Explain yuself / wha yu mean / when yu say half-caste.” Technique: Caribbean dialect, no punctuation, satirical examples. Theme: Racial identity; language as resistance. AO3: Agard born in Guyana; challenges the English establishment through dialect.

Catrin (Clarke): “the tight / Red rope of love.” Technique: Extended symbol (umbilical cord/rope), two-stanza structure. Theme: Mother-child conflict; love as struggle. AO3: Clarke writing from personal experience of motherhood.

War Photographer (Satyamurti): “The reassurance of the viewfinder.” Technique: Metaphor (camera as barrier). Theme: Moral dilemma of witnessing vs documenting. AO3: Role of media in representing conflict.

Belfast Confetti (Carson): “It was raining exclamation marks.” Technique: Punctuation as shrapnel metaphor, fragmented form. Theme: Violence shattering language and identity. AO3: The Troubles in Northern Ireland; street names from the Crimean War layering historical conflicts.

The Class Game (Casey): “How can you tell what class I’m from?” Technique: Listing, direct address, working-class dialect. Theme: Class prejudice. AO3: Casey’s working-class background; British class system.

Poppies (Weir): “hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind.” Technique: Enjambment, textile extended metaphor. Theme: Mother’s grief; private loss. AO3: Commissioned for Remembrance Day; draws on mothers of serving soldiers.

No Problem (Zephaniah): “I am not de problem.” Technique: Refrain, dub rhythm. Theme: Confronting racism with defiance. AO3: British-Jamaican identity; dub poetry tradition.

What Were They Like? (Levertov): “Sir, laughter is bitter to the burned mouth.” Technique: Q&A structure, past tense. Theme: Cultural erasure; anti-war protest. AO3: Written during the Vietnam War as protest; American poet opposing US military action.

Model Paragraph

Here is a model comparative paragraph for the question: “Compare how the poets present the effects of conflict on individuals in Exposure and one other poem.”

Key Fact

Model: Both Owen in Exposure and Weir in Poppies present individuals trapped by the effects of conflict, yet while Owen portrays the soldier’s physical suffering, Weir portrays the mother’s emotional torment. Owen’s half-rhymes (“knive us / nervous”) deny the reader a satisfying resolution, creating a dissonant, unsettling atmosphere that mirrors the soldiers’ own denied expectations of heroism. In contrast, Weir uses flowing enjambment (“hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind”) to create a breathless, reaching quality — the mother’s grief overflows the line just as it overflows her ability to contain it. Contextually, Owen draws on first-hand trench experience to expose the reality that soldiers’ greatest enemy was the weather, not the opposing army; Weir, writing for a Remembrance Day commission, gives voice to the mothers who are often invisible in war narratives.

Final Checklist: Before You Start Writing

Use this mental checklist in the exam:

  • Read the named poem carefully — underline key phrases, note techniques in the margin.
  • Identify the theme in the question — circle it. Every paragraph must link back to this theme.
  • Choose your comparison poem — pick the one you know best that connects to the theme. Write down 3–4 quotations from memory immediately, before you forget.
  • Plan 4–5 comparison points — each one should address the theme through a different angle (language, form, structure, imagery, context).
  • Write — every paragraph compares both poems. Integrate AO3 throughout, not at the end.
  • Proofread — check you have used subject terminology, comparison connectives, and have not just retold the poems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the final minutes, re-read your response and check: (1) Does every paragraph mention both poems? (2) Have I analysed how (technique + effect), not just described what? (3) Have I included at least two context points (one per poem)? (4) Does every paragraph link back to the theme in the question? If you can answer yes to all four, you have written a strong comparison.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Spend 5 minutes planning: choose your poem, jot down quotations, plan 4–5 comparison points.
  • Every paragraph must compare both poems, integrating AO2 (methods) and AO3 (context) throughout.
  • Use the quotation bank to build confidence across all 15 poems, but focus your deep revision on 4–5 chosen poems with memorised quotations, techniques and effects.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present attitudes towards authority in The Charge of the Light Brigade and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Strong choices: Half-caste (challenging racial authority), Cousin Kate (challenging patriarchal authority), What Were They Like? (challenging military/political authority). Analyses Tennyson's dual attitude — celebrating soldiers' obedience ('Theirs not to reason why') while criticising command ('Someone had blundered'). Comparison poem analysed with equivalent depth. AO3 woven throughout: Tennyson's role as Poet Laureate, context of comparison poem.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison, basic analysis.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present the power of nature in Extract from The Prelude and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Strong choice: Exposure (nature as hostile enemy). Analyses Wordsworth's personification ('Strode after me') and blank verse creating awe vs Owen's personification ('merciless iced east winds') and half-rhyme creating dread. Explores how Wordsworth's nature is sublime and educational (the boy learns humility) vs Owen's nature is brutally lethal (soldiers die from cold). Romantic sublime vs WW1 realism.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

practice_questions.text: From memory, write three quotations from your best-prepared poem. For each, identify the technique and explain the effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Three accurate quotations, each with a precisely identified technique and a detailed explanation of effect. E.g. for Exposure: 1. 'merciless iced east winds that knive us' — personification; nature is weaponised, suggesting the soldiers' greatest enemy is the weather. 2. 'But nothing happens' — refrain; creates crushing futility through repetition. 3. 'Slowly our ghosts drag home' — metaphor; the soldiers are psychologically dead even before they die physically.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Three quotations with clear technique + effect.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Two quotations or limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): One quotation with basic comment.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present loss and grief in Poppies and Cousin Kate. You should compare language, form and structure, and consider contexts. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (16-20): Sustained comparison. Both speakers are women experiencing profound loss — Weir's mother losing a son to war, Rossetti's speaker losing innocence and status to exploitation. Weir's free verse and enjambment mirror uncontrolled emotion; Rossetti's ballad form places her in a folk tradition of wronged women. Weir's textile imagery ('pinned', 'crimped') connects domestic and military worlds; Rossetti's possessive similes ('wore me like a glove') reduce the speaker to an object. modern vs Victorian contexts; different social constraints on women's expression of grief.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear comparison with relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Limited.

practice_questions.text: Write a 5-minute exam plan for: 'Compare how the poets present the reality of violence in Belfast Confetti and one other poem.' Include: chosen poem, 4 comparison points, key quotations, and one AO3 point per poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Complete plan with all elements. E.g. Chosen poem: The Destruction of Sennacherib. Points: 1. Both present destruction, but Carson's is chaotic/urban, Byron's is divine/absolute. 2. Carson's fragmented form vs Byron's driving AABB couplets. 3. Carson's punctuation-as-shrapnel metaphor vs Byron's colour imagery (purple/gold → pale/chill). 4. Carson's unanswered questions vs Byron's certain, resolved narrative. Quotations: 'raining exclamation marks' (Carson), 'like the wolf on the fold' (Byron). Carson — the Troubles, personal experience; Byron — biblical source, Romantic fascination with power.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear plan with most elements.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Partial plan.
Lower band (1-2): Limited.

practice_questions.text: A student has 5 minutes left in the exam. What should they prioritise: writing another paragraph, or proofreading their existing response? Explain your answer with reference to the mark scheme.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
- If they have only 3-4 paragraphs, another paragraph adds more AO2 evidence and potentially a new comparison point (1 mark)
- If they have 4-5 paragraphs already, proofreading is more valuable — checking every paragraph compares both poems, checking terminology is used, checking quotations are accurate (1 mark)
- The mark scheme rewards sustained comparison and precise analysis over quantity — 4 strong paragraphs beat 6 weak ones (1 mark)
- Quick proofreading wins: add a comparison connective where one is missing, correct a misremembered quotation, add a context sentence (1 mark)
